WHAT THE CHANGE DOES (context, do not re-litigate the product decisions):
1. Retires a `Read(./.entire/metadata/**)` permission deny rule Entire used to install into Claude Code and Factory Droid configs. Install now REMOVES it instead of adding it; `entire doctor` detects+repairs; the SessionStart hook detects and prints a notice but deliberately does NOT write (because the config file is normally git-tracked, so a hook writing it would dirty the user's worktree).
2. Adds `clearFilesystemTranscript` so a session's staged `.entire/metadata/<id>/full.jsonl` is deleted after successful condensation (it previously leaked forever — ~460MB observed).

YOUR TASK — find only ALTITUDE problems.

Specifically evaluate:
- **Is the new `MetadataDenyRule`-specific machinery too narrow?** `permissions.go` names one specific retired rule throughout (`HasMetadataDenyRule`, `RemoveMetadataDenyRule`, `HasRetiredMetadataDenyRule`, `RepairRetiredMetadataDenyRule`). Should this instead be a general "retired/managed permission rules" mechanism keyed on a list, so the next retired rule is a one-line addition rather than a new set of functions? Weigh that against over-engineering for a hypothetical second rule — say which way you land and why.
- **Is `PermissionConfigOwner` the right abstraction, at the right layer?** It lives in the `agent` package and is implemented by exactly two agents. Is there an existing agent-capability interface it should have extended instead? Check `cmd/entire/cli/agent/capabilities.go` for the established capability pattern and whether something like `HookSupport` or `HookFreshness` already covers config access.
- **Is the migration in the right place?** Removal happens inside `InstallHooks` in each agent package (duplicated per agent) plus in `doctor.go` plus a detect-only path in `lifecycle.go`. Is there a single deeper seam where a "config migration" belongs — e.g. alongside the existing stale-hook migration (`installHookEntries` / `dropStaleEntireHooks`), which solves the same class of problem (config written by an older CLI version)? Read those and say whether the new removal should have been folded into that existing mechanism rather than sitting beside it.
- **`clearFilesystemTranscript` vs `clearFilesystemPrompt`**: these are now two sibling functions doing "release a staged metadata file after condensation", called back-to-back at one site. Is the right altitude a single "release staged session metadata" operation, rather than one function per filename that every future staged file must be added to? Note the guard/lifetime differences between prompt and transcript if they make separation correct.
- Special cases layered on shared infrastructure anywhere else in the diff.

Use Grep/Read freely to read the existing mechanisms before judging. Do NOT recommend generalizing something without first reading the existing mechanism you think it should join.

Report ONLY real findings, each as:
- file:line
- one-line summary
- the concrete cost (what future change becomes fragile or repetitive)
- the deeper/more general implementation you'd prefer, and an honest note on whether it's worth it now

If the altitude is right, say so plainly and explain briefly why. Do not pad. Do not report correctness bugs — a separate review covers those.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).

- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.

+package agent

+import (

+// MetadataDenyRule is the Read deny rule Entire used to install into agent
+// permission configs to keep an agent from reading `.entire/metadata`.
+//
+// It is no longer installed, and `entire enable` and `entire doctor` remove it.
+// The constant survives because removing it is now the migration, so the exact
+// string still has to be recognisable — and because it is what identifies the
+// rule as ours: a rule byte-identical to this one was written by Entire, so
+// deleting it takes nothing the user chose.
+//
+// Why it went, in order of weight:
+//
+//   - A `deny` rule is a hard block, not a hint. Rules resolve deny → ask →
+//     allow, first match wins, and a deny rule cannot carry allowlist
+//     exceptions, so there is no way to soften it. Claude Code applies Read
+//     deny rules to file-reading Bash commands too, so a recursive grep from
+//     the repo root — or a command that merely names the path — is refused and
+//     has to be approved by hand. That defeats unattended/auto permission
+//     modes for a whole class of ordinary commands.
+//   - It guarded a staging buffer, not a store. `.entire/metadata/<session>`
+//     holds a `full.jsonl` that is rewritten from the agent's own transcript on
+//     every Stop and deleted once the session is condensed. The durable copy
+//     lives in the checkpoint tree, which no permission rule covers: the same
+//     transcript is readable with `git show entire/checkpoints/v1:...`.
+//   - It was mostly redundant. `.entire/.gitignore` already ignores
+//     `metadata/`, and Claude Code's Grep skips gitignored files, so the
+//     accidental-bulk-read case that motivated the rule was already covered.
+//     Glob does not respect gitignore, but Glob returns names, not content.
+//
+// Deliberately NOT replaced with a PreToolUse hook on Read: that fires a
+// subprocess for every file the agent reads, on a hook path that is already the
+// dominant cost of a turn.
+const MetadataDenyRule = "Read(./.entire/metadata/**)"
+
+// HasMetadataDenyRule reports whether rawPermissions still carries the retired
+// metadata deny rule. Used by the diagnostics that tell a user why they are
+// being asked to approve ordinary commands; it does not mutate anything.
+func HasMetadataDenyRule(rawPermissions map[string]json.RawMessage) bool {
+	rules, ok := denyRules(rawPermissions)
+	if !ok {
+		return false
+	}
+	return slices.Contains(rules, MetadataDenyRule)
+}
+
+// RemoveMetadataDenyRule drops the retired metadata deny rule from
+// rawPermissions, mutating it in place, and reports whether anything changed.
+//
+// Only the exact MetadataDenyRule string is removed, so every other deny rule —
+// including one a user wrote — is preserved. An empty `deny` array is deleted
+// rather than left behind, so a config Entire fully owned goes back to holding
+// no permissions block at all instead of an empty one.
+//
+// A `deny` value that will not parse as a string array is left untouched: it is
+// not ours, and rewriting what we cannot read is worse than leaving it.
+func RemoveMetadataDenyRule(rawPermissions map[string]json.RawMessage) (bool, error) {
+	rules, ok := denyRules(rawPermissions)
+	if !ok {
+		return false, nil
+	}
+	kept := make([]string, 0, len(rules))
+	for _, rule := range rules {
+		if rule != MetadataDenyRule {
+			kept = append(kept, rule)
+		}
+	}
+	if len(kept) == len(rules) {
+		return false, nil
+	}
+	if len(kept) == 0 {
+		delete(rawPermissions, "deny")
+		return true, nil
+	}
+	denyJSON, err := json.Marshal(kept)
+	if err != nil {
+		return false, fmt.Errorf("failed to marshal permissions.deny: %w", err)
+	}
+	rawPermissions["deny"] = denyJSON
+	return true, nil
+}
+
+// denyRules parses rawPermissions["deny"] as a string array. ok is false when
+// the key is absent or holds something else, which both mean "nothing here for
+// us to act on".
+func denyRules(rawPermissions map[string]json.RawMessage) (rules []string, ok bool) {
+	denyRaw, present := rawPermissions["deny"]
+	if !present {
+		return nil, false
+	}
+	if err := json.Unmarshal(denyRaw, &rules); err != nil {
+		return nil, false
+	}
+	return rules, true
+}
+
+// PermissionConfigOwner is implemented by an agent that keeps Entire-managed
+// entries in a JSON config with a top-level "permissions" object. It exists so
+// the shared diagnostics and the retired-rule migration can inspect and repair
+// that block without knowing where each agent keeps its config.
+//
+// Implemented by Claude Code (.claude/settings.json) and Factory AI Droid
+// (.factory/settings.json) — the two agents Entire ever wrote MetadataDenyRule
+// into.
+type PermissionConfigOwner interface {
+	// PermissionConfig returns the agent's permission-bearing config file for
+	// the current worktree. It does not create anything.
+	PermissionConfig(ctx context.Context) (*HookConfigFile, error)
+}
+
+// AsPermissionConfigOwner returns ag as a PermissionConfigOwner when it keeps a
+// permissions block Entire may have written into.
+func AsPermissionConfigOwner(ag Agent) (PermissionConfigOwner, bool) {
+	owner, ok := ag.(PermissionConfigOwner)
+	return owner, ok
+}
+
+// HasRetiredMetadataDenyRule reports whether ag's config still carries the
+// retired deny rule. It is read-only and answers false for every reason that is
+// not a positive sighting — agent doesn't own a permissions config, file absent,
+// unreadable, or unparseable — because its only callers are diagnostics, and
+// telling a user their config is broken on the strength of a failed read is
+// worse than staying quiet.
+func HasRetiredMetadataDenyRule(ctx context.Context, ag Agent) bool {
+	owner, ok := AsPermissionConfigOwner(ag)
+	if !ok {
+		return false
+	}
+	cfg, err := owner.PermissionConfig(ctx)
+	if err != nil || !cfg.Exists() {
+		return false
+	}
+	_, rawPermissions, err := readPermissionsBlock(cfg)
+	if err != nil {
+		return false
+	}
+	return HasMetadataDenyRule(rawPermissions)
+}
+
+// RepairRetiredMetadataDenyRule removes the retired deny rule from ag's config
+// and reports whether the file was changed.
+//
+// Unlike the detector above, this one returns its errors: it is reached from
+// `entire doctor`, where a config that cannot be parsed is the answer the user
+// needs rather than something to swallow.
+func RepairRetiredMetadataDenyRule(ctx context.Context, ag Agent) (bool, error) {
+	owner, ok := AsPermissionConfigOwner(ag)
+	if !ok {
+		return false, nil
+	}
+	cfg, err := owner.PermissionConfig(ctx)
+	if err != nil {
+		return false, err //nolint:wrapcheck // the agent's accessor already names its file
+	}
+	if !cfg.Exists() {
+		return false, nil
+	}
+	rawSettings, rawPermissions, err := readPermissionsBlock(cfg)
+	if err != nil {
+		return false, err
+	}
+	changed, err := RemoveMetadataDenyRule(rawPermissions)
+	if err != nil || !changed {
+		return false, err
+	}
+
+	// An emptied permissions block is deleted rather than written back as {}, so
+	// a config Entire fully owned ends up as it was before Entire touched it.
+	if len(rawPermissions) == 0 {
+		delete(rawSettings, "permissions")
+	} else {
+		permJSON, marshalErr := jsonutil.MarshalWithNoHTMLEscape(rawPermissions)
+		if marshalErr != nil {
+			return false, fmt.Errorf("failed to marshal permissions for %s: %w", cfg.Path(), marshalErr)
+		}
+		rawSettings["permissions"] = permJSON
+	}
+
+	output, err := jsonutil.MarshalIndentWithNewline(rawSettings, "", "  ")
+	if err != nil {
+		return false, fmt.Errorf("failed to marshal %s: %w", cfg.Path(), err)
+	}
+	if err := cfg.Write(output, 0o600); err != nil {
+		return false, fmt.Errorf("failed to write %s: %w", cfg.Path(), err)
+	}
+	return true, nil
+}
+
+// readPermissionsBlock reads cfg and returns its top-level fields plus the
+// "permissions" object. rawPermissions is always non-nil so callers can index
+// it without a nil check.
+func readPermissionsBlock(cfg *HookConfigFile) (rawSettings, rawPermissions map[string]json.RawMessage, err error) {
+	data, err := cfg.Read()
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to read %s: %w", cfg.Path(), err)
+	}
+	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &rawSettings); err != nil {
+		return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to parse %s: %w", cfg.Path(), err)
+	}
+	if rawSettings == nil {
+		rawSettings = make(map[string]json.RawMessage)
+	}
+	if permRaw, ok := rawSettings["permissions"]; ok {
+		if err := json.Unmarshal(permRaw, &rawPermissions); err != nil {
+			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to parse permissions in %s: %w", cfg.Path(), err)
+		}
+	}
+	if rawPermissions == nil {
+		rawPermissions = make(map[string]json.RawMessage)
+	}
+	return rawSettings, rawPermissions, nil
+}

+		wantDeny    []string

+		// an empty slice: an empty `deny` array left behind is config litter.
+		wantDenyAbsent bool

+			name:           "sole rule removes the whole key",
+			input:          `{"deny":["Read(./.entire/metadata/**)"]}`,
+			wantChanged:    true,
+			wantDenyAbsent: true,
+		},

+			input:       `{"deny":["Bash(rm -rf *)","Read(./.entire/metadata/**)","Read(./.env)"]}`,
+			wantChanged: true,
+			wantDeny:    []string{"Bash(rm -rf *)", "Read(./.env)"},
+		},
+		{
+			name:        "absent rule is a no-op",
+			input:       `{"deny":["Bash(rm -rf *)"]}`,
+			wantChanged: false,
+			wantDeny:    []string{"Bash(rm -rf *)"},
+		},
+		{
+			name:           "no deny key at all",
+			input:          `{"allow":["Read(**)"]}`,
+			wantChanged:    false,
+			wantDenyAbsent: true,
+		},
+		{
+			// Duplicates are possible in a hand-edited config; every copy goes.
+			name:           "every duplicate is removed",
+			input:          `{"deny":["Read(./.entire/metadata/**)","Read(./.entire/metadata/**)"]}`,
+			wantChanged:    true,
+			wantDenyAbsent: true,
+		},
+		{

+			// wrote is ours to delete.
+			name:        "a similar-but-different rule is left alone",
+			input:       `{"deny":["Read(./.entire/metadata/**/*)","Read(.entire/metadata/**)"]}`,
+			wantChanged: false,
+			wantDeny:    []string{"Read(./.entire/metadata/**/*)", "Read(.entire/metadata/**)"},
+		},

+			if tt.wantDeny != nil {

Now I have enough grounding in both the new code and the existing mechanisms it touches. Here is the altitude review.

## Overall verdict

Altitude is right almost everywhere in this diff. The two places that most invite a "special case" critique — `PermissionConfigOwner` and the doctor/lifecycle/InstallHooks split — actually mirror established patterns in this codebase closely enough that generalizing further would be inventing structure that doesn't exist yet anywhere else. One real finding, on `clearFilesystemTranscript`/`clearFilesystemPrompt`.

## Findings

**1. `clearFilesystemTranscript` and `clearFilesystemPrompt` should be one function, not two.**
- `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:1596-1645` (both functions plus their `session*Name` helpers), called only from `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:1483-1486`
- The two functions are never called independently — the sole call site invokes them back-to-back under the exact same `if len(state.FilesTouched) == 0` guard, with identical signatures `(ctx, sessionID)`, both best-effort, both opening their own `entiredir.OpenForRead(ctx)`. The transcript function's own doc comment even says it's "called from the same place (and under the same guard) as `clearFilesystemPrompt`" — the code already documents that these are one operation, not two. The guard is identical for a real reason, not coincidentally: if carry-forward files remain, both prompt.txt and full.jsonl must survive for the next condensation to read, since nothing guarantees a Stop event refreshes them first.
- Cost: every future staged file (there's a real precedent for growth — `TranscriptFileNameLegacy` already needed a second remove call bolted directly into `clearFilesystemTranscript` rather than getting its own function) means another near-duplicate function, another doc comment repeating the same guard/lifetime rationale, and another `entiredir.OpenForRead` call at the same call site. The path-building helper pattern (`entiredir.MustName(paths.SessionMetadataDirFromSessionID(sessionID)) + "/" + paths.XFileName`) is already repeated three times (`sessionPromptName`, `sessionTranscriptName`, and the inline legacy path) with no shared helper.
- Preferred shape: a single `clearFilesystemStagedFiles(ctx, sessionID)` that opens the root once and removes `paths.PromptFileName`, `paths.TranscriptFileName`, and `paths.TranscriptFileNameLegacy` from one resolved metadata-dir name. This is a small, low-risk, worthwhile change now (not speculative generalization) — the duplication already exists at exactly 2x, the call site already proves they're one operation, and the fix is a few lines.

## Non-findings (reviewed and judged correctly placed)

**`MetadataDenyRule`-specific machinery (`permissions.go:43-172`).** Narrow, named after the one retired rule throughout (`HasMetadataDenyRule`, `RemoveMetadataDenyRule`, `HasRetiredMetadataDenyRule`, `RepairRetiredMetadataDenyRule`). This would need duplicating (new constant + 4 functions + 2 call sites) if Entire ever retires a second deny rule. But there's no existing precedent in this codebase for a declarative "list of retired things" migration registry — the sibling mechanism this most resembles, `dropStaleEntireHooks`, is itself called with explicit per-call-site `want ...string` arguments, not driven by a table. The doc comment on `MetadataDenyRule` also argues Entire is moving away from deny rules as a mechanism entirely (blunt, no allowlist exceptions, redundant with `.gitignore`), which makes a second instance of this specific shape less likely than it might first appear. Building a generalized "retired permission rules" list now, before a second member exists, would be speculative; the refactor is contained to one ~170-line file if it's ever needed. Right call to leave it concrete.

**`PermissionConfigOwner` (`permissions.go:114-131`).** This is a new one-method optional interface in the `agent` package, gated by direct type assertion (`AsPermissionConfigOwner`) rather than through `CapabilityDeclarer`/`DeclaredCaps`. Checked against `capabilities.go`: this is exactly the established pattern for built-in-only capabilities with no external-agent-protocol equivalent — `AsHookFreshness`, `AsModelExtractor`, `AsSessionEndBudgeter`, `AsToolInvocationScanner` etc. all resolve by bare type assertion with a comment explaining why no declared-capability gate applies. `HookSupport` was not extended with a `PermissionConfig` method — correctly: only 2 of the many `HookSupport` implementers have a deny-rule-bearing config, and piling an optional concern onto a widely-implemented interface is the anti-pattern this codebase already avoids elsewhere (`ProtectedFilesProvider`, `TranscriptPreparer`, `TranscriptFetcher` are all separate narrow interfaces for the same reason). `PermissionConfig()` returns the existing shared `*agent.HookConfigFile` type rather than inventing new I/O — it's a thin accessor over machinery that already existed (`claudeHookConfig`/`factoryHookConfig` were already private functions returning this type; the interface just exposes them polymorphically). Right layer, right shape. (Minor, non-blocking nit: `PermissionConfigOwner` doesn't embed `Agent` the way every sibling capability interface does, and it lives in `permissions.go` rather than alongside the interface definitions in `agent.go` / helpers in `capabilities.go`. Neither affects behavior or correctness; not worth a separate change.)

**Migration location (`InstallHooks` in both agents, `UninstallHooks` in both agents, `doctor.go:826-863`, `lifecycle.go:196-207`).** Not duplicated logic — one shared pure function (`agent.RemoveMetadataDenyRule`, operating on an in-memory `map[string]json.RawMessage`) is called directly from each agent's `InstallHooks`/`UninstallHooks` because those functions already hold `rawPermissions` mid-flow as part of a larger read-modify-write that also touches hooks; a shared higher-level orchestrator (`agent.RepairRetiredMetadataDenyRule`, which does its own read-then-write) is used by `doctor.go` and probed read-only via `agent.HasRetiredMetadataDenyRule` from `lifecycle.go`, both of which don't already have a loaded settings file in hand. This split avoids a doctor-driven write colliding with an install-driven write to the same file. It was correctly *not* folded into `installHookEntries`/`dropStaleEntireHooks`: those operate on a structurally different JSON shape (arrays of hook matchers, matched by command string) and there's no existing generalized "config migration" seam in this codebase to join — `installHookEntries` itself is hand-written per hook type, not table-driven. `doctor.go`'s new `checkRetiredDenyRule` reuses the exact same iterate-agents-with-hooks-installed-and-probe-a-capability shape as the pre-existing `checkHookDrift`, and `lifecycle.go`'s SessionStart notice (`retired_deny_rule_notice.go`) matches the pre-existing `codexSessionStartWarning` pattern (its own small file, a pure string-returning function, called conditionally via `message +=`). Both are the established altitude for this class of check/notice, not new machinery.

No other special-cases-bolted-onto-shared-infrastructure were found elsewhere in the diff.
